title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of K-12 Education: What Do Parents Want? | Institute for Family Studies
gist: IFS/YouGov survey of 2,000 U.S. K-12 parents (Jul-Aug 2026) finds strong, bipartisan and cross-class resistance to AI in schools: 56% want it fully blocked, 75% back pauses like NYC and LA, and most expect more harm than benefit. The report recommends a 'computer lab' model, limiting AI before high school, outcome-verified ed tech procurement, and a return to books and handwriting, warning that the Washington/Silicon Valley push for classroom AI is on a collision course with parents.

insights.claim: Nearly 4 in 10 U.S. K-12 students attend schools where AI use is explicitly allowed or required, 15% attend schools that officially block it, and 45% attend schools that have taken no official action.
insights.speaker: Jared Hayden
insights.so_what: Nearly half of schools have no AI policy yet, so the policy-setting window for ed-tech AI vendors is still open and contested.

themes.theme: Parental demand: less AI, later, in labs

insights.claim: 56% of K-12 parents want AI fully blocked in schools and another 26% want less AI than currently used, while only 13% want more and 6% want as much as possible.
insights.speaker: Jared Hayden
insights.so_what: Over 80% of the end-customer's stakeholders oppose expansion, a major demand headwind for K-12 AI products.
insights.quote: A majority (56%) of parents want AI fully blocked in schools, and another 26% want less AI in schools than is currently required or allowed.

insights.claim: Opposition to AI in schools shows class unanimity: about 3 in 4 of both the highest-educated and highest-earning parents want less AI or none, and roughly half of Republicans (52%) and Democrats (49%) want none at all.
insights.speaker: Jared Hayden
insights.so_what: Bipartisan, cross-class opposition makes restrictive policy politically easy and durable.
insights.quote: In sum, there is significant class unanimity on this issue.
insights.locator: While the highest-educated and the highest-earning

insights.claim: More than two-thirds of parents want AI introduced only in high school or later, or not at all; just 3% favor kindergarten and 9% elementary school.
insights.speaker: Jared Hayden
insights.so_what: Elementary/middle-school AI products face the weakest demand and highest regulatory risk.
insights.quote: Only 3% of parents believe that students should be using AI in kindergarten and only 9% want it introduced in elementary school.
insights.locator: 4. Parents want AI later

insights.claim: The most popular classroom model among parents (38%) is printed books and handwriting as primary media with AI confined to a computer lab; another 25% want books and handwriting only, and only 11% back the tablet-plus-AI model.
insights.speaker: Jared Hayden
insights.so_what: Points to demand shifts away from one-to-one devices toward shared hardware and print materials, negative for device/ed-tech vendors and positive for print publishers.
insights.quote: Only 11% of parents want this form of education for their kids.
insights.locator: 3. Many parents want deep changes

insights.claim: Conservatives (31%) are more likely than liberals (21%) to want to replace tablets with books and handwriting, but 37-38% of conservatives, moderates and liberals alike favor the books-first plus computer-lab compromise.
insights.speaker: Jared Hayden
insights.so_what: A centrist 'computer lab' compromise is the likely policy equilibrium.

themes.theme: Parents expect AI harms to outweigh benefits

insights.claim: 77% of parents say AI in schools will hurt learning, 79% say it will enable malicious behavior like cheating or AI-generated nudes of peers, and 73% say it will expose children to serious risks such as self-harm-encouraging chatbots.
insights.speaker: Jared Hayden
insights.so_what: Safety and liability concerns are the dominant frame, raising compliance costs and litigation risk for student-facing AI.

themes.theme: Policy backlash: pauses and accountability laws

insights.claim: New York City and Los Angeles paused student AI use in most K-12 classrooms, and the pause is supported by 75% of Republican and 72% of Democratic parents, so it is not a partisan policy.
insights.speaker: Jared Hayden
insights.so_what: Moratoria are likely to spread to other districts, slowing AI ed-tech sales.
insights.quote: 75% of Republican parents support the policy to pause AI in schools, as do 72% of Democratic parents
insights.locator: 6. A large majority of parents

insights.claim: State laws are restricting classroom tech: Nevada bans replacing school counselors with AI, Utah's Balance Act restricts ed tech in lower grades and generative AI, and Utah's SAFE Act requires independent verification of academic effectiveness and bans addictive design and emotion-analyzing AI.
insights.speaker: Jared Hayden
insights.so_what: Third-party efficacy and design rules raise the compliance bar for ed-tech vendors and could become a template for other states.

insights.claim: The authors recommend the FCC narrow E-Rate covered services, require vendors to prove learning outcomes and impose a regulated fee schedule, and propose a 'device buyback program' swapping Chromebooks for printed texts.

insights.so_what: Watch E-Rate review and state subsidies as direct revenue risks for school device and connectivity vendors.
